📌 Address Poisoning: Why Your Transaction History Can Lie

Main Points
⏺ Scammers plant look-alike addresses in your wallet history
⏺ One careless copy-paste sends your funds to them
⏺ This post explains how the trick works and how to avoid it



1️⃣ Core Idea — Attackers create an address that starts and ends with the same characters as one you use, then send you a tiny or zero-value transfer from it so it shows up in your history.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — Most people check only the first and last few characters, and many wallets shorten addresses on screen. Copying "the last address I used" from history is a habit scammers count on.
3️⃣ Example — You regularly send USDT to your exchange. A dust transfer arrives from an address that looks the same at a glance; next time you copy from history and pick the fake one.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Stablecoin transfers, wallets that display shortened addresses, and any payment you copy from recent activity instead of a saved contact.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — Never copy addresses from your transaction history. Use a saved address book, check the full address, and send a small test transfer before a large one.
Final Thoughts

Address poisoning doesn't hack your wallet — it hacks your attention. A few extra seconds of checking is the whole defense.

⚠️ Hong Kong SFC flags Hyperliquid as suspicious trading platform, can HYPE price hold $65? 

💭 Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has added decentralized derivatives exchange Hyperliquid to its list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms over concerns that it may be offering services in the jurisdiction without regulatory authorization. The SFC said Hyperliquid was not licensed and was suspected of operating a virtual asset trading platform in Hong Kong or “actively marketing its services to the Hong Kong public.”

📌 Hyperliquid (HYPE) showed a limited price reaction following the publication of the warning, trading at $68.48 during Thursday’s session, down 0.33% over 24 hours. However, the cryptocurrency remained 12.62% lower over the past month. Hong Kong introduced its licensing framework for centralized virtual asset trading platforms in June 2023, requiring operators conducting business in the city or actively targeting local investors to obtain regulatory authorization.

👀 The commission has previously worked with the Hong Kong Police Force to restrict access to websites associated with suspicious trading platforms. In March 2025, police took steps to block access to Linkbex’s website at the regulator’s request following complaints involving suspected investment fraud. The latest warning against Hyperliquid, however, contains no announcement of an internet service provider block, app-store removal, asset freeze or mandatory suspension of trading services. It does not specifically accuse the platform of fraud.

Premium Markup, Missing Ingredient

Britain bought explosives, marketed as improved C4, for Ukrainian attack drones, but its own tests found no detectable RDX, C4’s main explosive ingredient. 

The Financial Times reports that U.S. supplier Tripwire South instead supplied a cheaper PETN-based commercial explosive, charging $77 a pound for material bought at $40 to $45. That is a markup, and the figures do not show net profit.

Records covered roughly 32 tonnes. A separate contract provided for an initial 36 tonnes, with options taking the total to 204 tonnes at about £26.3 million. How much of that was delivered or paid for is not clear.

Founder Ryan Morris denies misrepresentation, and Britain’s Ministry of Defence says the material was fit for purpose. 

The procurement question is why a product sold as an upgrade remained acceptable after official tests contradicted its advertised composition. The supplier collected the markup. British taxpayers paid for the deal.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.

EVERY NIGHT, YOUR BRAIN SHRINKS SLIGHTLY TO WASH ITSELF. MOST PEOPLE NEVER REACH THE FREQUENCY THAT TURNS IT ON.

In 2012, neuroscientists discovered a hidden cleaning network inside the human skull called the Glymphatic System.

During the day, while you think, work, and process stress, your brain cells produce metabolic waste and toxic proteins.

That waste can only be flushed out at night—when your brain enters deep Delta wave sleep (0.5 to 4 Hz).

When you hit true Delta frequencies, your brain cells actually shrink by up to 60%, opening microscopic channels that allow cerebrospinal fluid to rush through and wash away the toxic buildup.
